extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, publishers, and aspiring sensitivity readers interested in how sensitivity reads are done
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and norms for doing sensitivity reads and for authors/editors commissioning them: scope of work, process, deliverables, limits, and emotional/ethical considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include sensitivity readers in normal editing process
rubrics_metrics.description: We should be included as a normal part of the editing process; we should be seen as just as crucial as say, a developmental or line editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocate that sensitivity readers be treated as a standard editorial role rather than an optional add-on; encourage publishers and authors to budget and plan for sensitivity reads in their workflow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and identity-specific expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Salt & Sage’s list of sensitivity and expert consultants lists the experiences I read for (e.g., biracial (Black/white) identity, queer identity, atheist identity…). This doesn’t mean that I speak for every member of these communities or that my expertise is perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which lived experiences you are offering feedback on, and include disclaimers that a reader’s perspective is one lived experience, not a universal authority for an entire community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intake: request, brief, and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The process starts when an author requests a sensitivity read (which can be general or a request for me specifically). Then, I receive their piece, what they’re looking for, and any concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require a clear brief from the author describing goals and specific worries so the reader can focus feedback appropriately; accept both general and targeted requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formats covered
rubrics_metrics.description: So far I’ve read everything from articles and short stories to graphic novels and picture books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to adapt methods and feedback to different formats (prose, YA, picture books, graphic novels, articles) because issues and solutions differ by form and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing and time estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: My pay is based on the length of the piece and the time required. On average, I spend about three weeks on each work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set expectations with authors about fees tied to length/complexity and provide realistic timelines (example: ~3 weeks) before starting work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading method: multiple passes with different focus
rubrics_metrics.description: This usually allows for me to read a text once as if I was an average reader (jotting down notes if anything particularly egregious jumps out) and then a couple of times more with a laser focus on the identities I read for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an initial holistic read to capture reader experience, then focused passes to identify identity-specific issues; document observations during each pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliverable: letter with findings and positive notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Lastly, I write a letter to the author with my findings. This always includes positive notes, as nearly every story has a strong element to it in one way or another. Sometimes, the notes are only positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a written report/letter that balances critique with praise; always note strengths as well as problems so feedback is constructive and actionable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough analysis when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: However, I often write a lengthy analysis of what the author should fix if they want to be more authentic or avoid offensive content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When problems are substantive, give a detailed, prioritized list of issues and concrete recommendations for revision rather than only surface-level comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasoning behind critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most important parts of being a sensitivity reader (and dare I say it, a thorough one) is providing reasoning behind your critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain why something is problematic (historical context, cultural meaning, harm potential) instead of simply labeling it offensive; this helps authors learn and avoid repeating mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and explain damaging tropes/stereotypes
rubrics_metrics.description: They aren’t familiar with damaging tropes, perhaps, or didn’t realize that what they wrote is tapping into a stereotype... example: a Black character described with words like “monstrous” and “beastial.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag stereotypes and tropes explicitly, show where language or plot choices echo harmful caricatures, and give examples of why these tropes are damaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide resources for further research
rubrics_metrics.description: Along with the recommendation... I also provide a list of resources for further research. I might include scholarly articles detailing the racial history of the 'brute' caricature, blog posts from Black authors about how to not write Black boys/men, examples of films that do this trope badly, of films that avoid it altogether...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include annotated resources (articles, blog posts, films, scholarly works, examples of better/worse portrayals) so authors can educate themselves and avoid future errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct factual errors and missing context
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing about experiences outside their own, I find that most authors simply don’t know what they don’t know. Oftentimes, they might just get the facts wrong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out concrete factual inaccuracies and missing cultural/contextual details, and suggest accurate alternatives or sources to verify facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to recommend major revision or overhaul
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes you just have to tell someone that their entire book should be overhauled if they want to avoid causing harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to recommend large-scale revisions when problems are systemic; communicate this clearly and compassionately, understanding the emotional impact on the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional labor and self-care considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: It can be emotionally draining to immerse yourself in problematic work... During one read I had to take a break and walk around after a particularly violent stereotype reared its head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge the emotional toll of the work, build in boundaries and downtime, and set expectations with clients about the potential need for breaks or limits on back-to-back projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allyship: hard work and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Being a good ally means doing the hard work and taking on that responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach the role with humility and commitment: offer constructive feedback, accept discomfort in giving tough critiques, and prioritize reducing harm over protecting authors' feelings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overclaim authority
rubrics_metrics.description: As Salt & Sage makes sure authors know, this doesn’t mean that I speak for every member of these communities or that my expertise is perfect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear statements about the limits of your perspective; suggest additional readers/consultants where appropriate to cover other viewpoints within a community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocate for normalization of sensitivity reads in publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Hopefully, as authors and readers continue to recognize the value of sensitivity readers, we can become a commonplace component of the publishing industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage industry stakeholders to normalize hiring sensitivity readers (including for self-published authors) and to incorporate sensitivity feedback into standard editorial workflows.
